analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and all its coverage protections, effective at the start of 2020.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill never advanced past its first committee referrals and died at the end of the 115th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 law in their entirety, effective January 1, 2020, restoring the legal landscape as if those laws had never passed. That means ending the Medicaid expansion, the marketplace subsidies, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, the rule letting young adults stay on a parent's plan, and the taxes that paid for it all. It was introduced by a single member with four cosponsors, sent to nine committees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households, who would stop paying the Affordable Care Act's Medicare surtax and the 3.8% tax on investment income; device manufacturers, insurers, drug makers, and tanning businesses, which would be freed from the law's fees and taxes; and healthy, higher-income buyers, who would no longer subsidize community-rated premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and health industry firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law, effective January 1, 2020, restoring prior law as if the ACA had never been enacted.
Exempts the bill's budgetary effects from the statutory PAYGO scorecards, so the fiscal cost of repeal would not automatically trigger the law's spending cuts.
Removes the ACA's taxes on health industries — including the medical device tax, health insurer fee, and tanning tax — and the additional Medicare taxes on high earners' wages and investment income.

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of people who gained coverage or protections under the law: the roughly 20 million covered by the Medicaid expansion and marketplace subsidies, people with pre-existing conditions who would again be denied or priced out of insurance, seniors who would pay more as the Medicare prescription-drug coverage gap reopened, and young adults who would lose access to a parent's plan. The bill text does not replace any of these provisions.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and low-income households

drawbacks.text: It repeals the ACA with no replacement, so every coverage expansion, consumer protection, and benefit would end at once on January 1, 2020, including protections for pre-existing conditions and the ban on annual and lifetime coverage limits.

Restoring pre-ACA law would reopen the Medicare 'donut hole' prescription-drug gap and end the requirement that insurers cover essential health benefits, raising costs for seniors and anyone buying their own insurance.
Exempting the bill from statutory PAYGO scorecards means the large deficit impact of repealing the ACA's taxes and spending would not trigger the law's automatic offsets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a narrow set of payers — high-income households facing the Medicare surtax and investment-income tax, and industries facing ACA fees — while the costs fall on millions of people whose coverage and protections depend on the law. Because the bill repeals without replacing anything, an honest supporter has to acknowledge that the people who gained coverage since 2014 would lose it, and the budget rule exemption only makes the fiscal cost harder to track.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to nine House committees and three subcommittees, where nothing further happened; it never got a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Flores introduced the bill on January 9, 2017, with four Republican cosponsors, in the opening days of a Congress where repeal of the Affordable Care Act was a stated majority goal.

It was referred to nine full committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Rules, House Administration, Appropriations, and Budget — a referral structure that fragments a bill across so many jurisdictions that it is very hard to move.

In late January and early February 2017 it was referred to subcommittees on health and on Indian and Alaska Native affairs, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
Separate, broader repeal legislation moved through the same Congress in 2017, and this narrower bill never received consideration of its own.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 20-plus million people covered by the ACA's expansions and everyone with a pre-existing condition kept their protections, simply because the bill never advanced; high earners and health industry firms lost the tax repeal it would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People covered by the ACA kept their protections

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat supported it; the bill never reached a vote, so there are no roll-call numbers to break down.

industries.note: Repeal ends the additional Medicare tax on wages over $200,000 and the 3.8% net investment income tax, both of which fall on high earners and help finance coverage subsidies. The gain comes directly from undoing the law's funding.

Repeal eliminates the health insurer fee but also wipes out the individual mandate and the marketplace and Medicaid expansions that brought insurers millions of subsidized customers. Insurers lose the fee while losing a large government-created customer base.
Losing the Medicaid expansion and subsidized coverage would sharply increase uncompensated care, which hospitals absorb. Hospitals' financial interest here ran alongside keeping people covered.
Repeal eliminates the 2.3% excise tax on medical devices, one of the ACA's financing mechanisms. The industry's gain comes from removing a revenue source for public coverage.

Repeal ends the Medicaid drug rebate expansion and the requirement that manufacturers close the Medicare coverage-gap discount, removing industry obligations. But it also ends the coverage expansions that increased drug sales.
Repeal eliminates the 10% tanning tax, another ACA financing mechanism.
